articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals in Latest Iran-Related Action
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on November 6, 2026. This action targets individuals and entities involved in activities supporting the Iranian regime.

Further details regarding the specific individuals and entities designated, as well as the nature of their activities, are available on the OFAC website. These designations aim to increase pressure on Iran and disrupt its illicit networks.
This latest round of sanctions underscores the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to countering Iran's destabilizing activities and its pursuit of weapons proliferation.

articles.headline: OFAC Sanctions Global Scam Networks, Cuban Entities, and Publishes Cuba-Related Determination
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) on November 5, 2026, announced a series of designations targeting cyber-related and transnational criminal organizations, alongside new sanctions related to Cuba. This action includes the publication of a Cuba-related determination pursuant to Executive Order 14404, specifically targeting the electronics, manufacturing, marine, and technology sectors of the Cuban economy.

The designations against transnational criminal organizations aim to disrupt global scam networks involved in cyber-enabled fraud, money laundering, and human trafficking. These measures build on previous actions against groups like the Cambodia-based Prince Group Transnational Criminal Organization.

The Cuba-related sanctions expand restrictions on entities and individuals linked to Cuba's military and oil sector, including two individuals, five companies, and two vessels. This move is part of an ongoing effort to pressure the Cuban authorities and limit their illicit activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran-Related Designations, Updates Listings, Publishes Alert, and Amends Venezuela GL
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations and updates to existing Iran-related listings on November 4, 2026. Concurrently, OFAC published an Iran-related alert titled 'Iranian Shadow Fleet Reliance on False Flags for Sanctions Evasion,' highlighting the risks of providing services to vessels using deceptive practices to circumvent sanctions.

The alert emphasizes that false flags, either from fraudulent registries or falsely claimed by vessels, create a veneer of legitimacy for sanctions evasion. OFAC warns of substantial risks of designation or penalties for those providing services to such vessels.

In a separate but related action, OFAC also issued Venezuela-related General License 5AA, authorizing certain transactions related to the Petróleos de Venezuela, S.A. 2020 8.5 Percent Bond on or after December 18, 2026, and amended Frequently Asked Question 595.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License for Wind Down of Transactions
body: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued Iran General License FF-1 on October 29, 2026. This general license specifically authorizes the wind down of transactions involving the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance.

This action provides a limited period for U.S. persons to conclude certain transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under Iran sanctions regulations. The issuance of a wind-down general license typically precedes or accompanies new designations or restrictions, allowing for an orderly cessation of activities.
The details of the authorized wind-down period and the scope of transactions covered by General License FF-1 are outlined in the official publication on OFAC's website.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities and Individuals in North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations on October 28, 2026, targeting individuals and entities connected to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC).

The North Korea-related designations include Russian and North Korean nationals linked to entities such as LIMITED LIABILITY COMPANY ALIS, CHINYONG INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY COOPERATION COMPANY, and FIRST FINANCIAL AND TECHNICAL DEVELOPMENT CENTER, which are involved in financial and insurance activities.

For the Democratic Republic of the Congo, the designations include Rwanda's Ministry of Defence and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a Kigali-based financial institution. These actions aim to address destabilizing activities and human rights abuses in the region.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks Settles with OFAC for $1.5 Million Over Russia Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced a $1,529,685 settlement with Extreme Networks, Inc., a North Carolina-based cloud networking solutions provider, on October 27, 2026. The settlement resolves nine apparent violations of the Ukraine-/Russia-Related Sanctions Regulations.

Between September 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and services to Joint Stock Company (JSC) Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA), a Russian defense manufacturer. MMZA was deemed a blocked person due to its majority ownership by designated entity JSC Concern Almaz Antey, even though MMZA itself was not on the SDN List at the time of the transactions.

OFAC determined that the apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious. The settlement amount reflects this determination, and the company has agreed to maintain a sanctions compliance program for at least five years. The Department of Justice also resolved a parallel investigation with a non-prosecution agreement.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) amended several Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) on October 26, 2026. These amendments are part of OFAC's ongoing review to ensure its published guidance remains current and clear.

The updated FAQs cover topics related to blocking and rejecting transactions, as well as filing reports with OFAC. Key areas addressed include distinguishing between a customer inquiry and a payment instruction, when to reject versus block a transaction, and the procedures and deadlines for reporting blocked property and rejected transactions.
These revisions are crucial for financial institutions and other entities subject to OFAC regulations to ensure proper compliance with sanctions requirements and reporting obligations.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Iran-Related Designations, Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations, and Publishes New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new Iran-related designations on October 21, 2026. Simultaneously, OFAC removed certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea from its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List.

Specifically, Chinese national Lu Hezheng and two Chinese entities, Shanghai Moxing Cultural Media Co. Ltd. and Shanghai Hongman Cartoon and Animation Design Studio, were delisted under the North Korea sanctions program. Belarusian national Andrei Alekseevich Rybakov was also delisted from the Belarus sanctions program.
In addition to these changes, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended several Frequently Asked Questions, providing updated guidance for various transactions.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues PAIPA Designations and Associated General Licenses
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) on October 19, 2026. These designations are aimed at safeguarding American intellectual property from theft and illicit acquisition.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also issued associated General Licenses. These licenses typically authorize certain transactions or activities that would otherwise be prohibited under the PAIPA sanctions program, providing specific carve-outs or wind-down periods.
The details of the designated entities and individuals, along with the scope and conditions of the associated General Licenses, are available on OFAC's recent actions page.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ for Earthquake Relief
body: The Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) issued Venezuela-related General License 60A on October 16, 2026. This amended general license specifically authorizes transactions related to earthquake relief efforts in Venezuela.
In addition to the general license, OFAC also issued an amended Frequently Asked Question, FAQ 1263, to provide further clarification and guidance regarding the authorized activities.
This action aims to facilitate humanitarian aid and support for disaster relief in Venezuela, demonstrating a targeted approach to sanctions implementation that allows for essential assistance.

body: Extreme Networks, Inc., a cloud networking solutions provider, has agreed to pay $1,529,685 to the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) to settle apparent violations of sanctions regulations.

The settlement addresses nine instances between September 2018 and March 2022 where Extreme Networks exported networking equipment and services to a Russian defense manufacturer, Joint Stock Company (JSC) Moskovskiy Mashinostroitelniy Zavod Avangard (MMZA). MMZA was considered a blocked person due to its majority ownership by a designated entity, JSC Concern Almaz Antey.
OFAC determined that the violations were egregious but voluntarily self-disclosed. A parallel investigation by the Department of Justice also resulted in a non-prosecution agreement.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.
